name: Massachusetts
scope: Alimony after divorce under the Alimony Reform Act (M.G.L. c. 208, §§ 48-55): general term, rehabilitative, reimbursement and transitional alimony; duration limits apply to general term alimony.
formulaText: Except for reimbursement alimony or unusual circumstances, alimony should generally not exceed the recipient's need or 30-35% of the difference between the parties' gross incomes when the order issues (M.G.L. c. 208, § 53(b), as explained by the Probate and Family Court). Gross income is the Child Support Guidelines definition, excluding capital gains, dividends and interest from assets already divided, and income already used for a child support order. The new spouse's income of a remarried payer is not considered.
durationText: General term alimony maximum (M.G.L. c. 208, § 49(b), per the Probate and Family Court): marriages of 5 years or less: 50% of the number of months married; 10 years or less: 60%; 15 years or less: 70%; 20 years or less: 80%; more than 20 years: as long as the judge finds fair. Alimony normally ends on the death of either spouse, remarriage of the recipient, or the payer reaching full retirement age; cohabitation for at least 3 months can reduce or end it.
eligibilityText: Alimony is paid by a spouse able to pay to a spouse in need; the court weighs length of marriage, age, health, income and employability, economic and non-economic contributions, marital lifestyle, ability to maintain it, lost economic opportunity and other factors. Reimbursement and transitional alimony are only for marriages of no more than 5 years.

facts.text: General term alimony normally stops when the payer reaches full retirement age, unless the judge orders otherwise.
Living with a partner for at least 3 months can reduce or end the recipient's alimony.
Reimbursement and transitional alimony are reserved to marriages of no more than 5 years.
When a remarried payer's alimony is reviewed for an increase, the new spouse's income is not considered.
